SATE: Transferable Spin-Adapted Neural Wavefunctions

Timothy Sereda Affiliation: Primateria  2University of South Dakota  3Stanford University    Pallas Chou    Morris Hsieh Affiliation: Primateria  2University of South Dakota  3Stanford University    Emerson Hsieh Affiliation: Primateria  2University of South Dakota  3Stanford University
Abstract

Accurate prediction of molecular reactivity requires both accurate and computationally efficient description of electron correlation and spin across various molecular geometries and electronic states. We introduce SATE, a spin-adapted transferable neural wavefunction architecture with effective core potentials. SATE combines a transferable neural wavefunction, the spin-adapted antisymmetrization method, and effective core potentials into a single foundation model architecture pretrained on compositions containing selected elements from hydrogen to bromine. After pretraining and adaptation, our model is able to predict 3d transition-metal spin-state gaps, bond dissociation energies, ionization energies, and a reaction energy with absolute deviations of 2.1–8.7 mHa from reference values, based on two-seed means. Effective core potentials reduce the number of explicitly treated electrons, while spin-adapted antisymmetrization enforces the prescribed total spin. By testing our model with 3d transition metal chemistry, we evaluate our model’s description of strong electron correlation and competing electronic states in such systems. We find that pretraining improves most tested component energies at matched adaptation budgets, while improvements in spin-state gaps, dissociation energies, ionization energies and the reaction energy remain system dependent. Ultimately, our work lays the foundation for more accurate and transferable modeling of molecular systems by combining the computational efficiency of effective core potentials with explicit control over total spin.

Introduction

Accurate predictions of molecular reactivity require electronic structure methods that remain reliable as bonds break and competing electronic states change in energy. Transition-metal compounds present a distinct computational challenge. Because their partially occupied d shells often generate near-degenerate electronic configurations and multiple low-lying spin states, predicting accurate relative energies requires a method that simultaneously accounts for both static and dynamic electron correlation. 41. The accuracy of density functional theory (DFT) and single-reference coupled-cluster, such as coupled cluster with singles, doubles, and perturbative triples (CCSD(T)), depends on the system and electronic state. For example, benchmark studies on DFT and CCSD(T) show substantial method dependence in transition-metal spin-state energetics 35. Multireference approaches can describe this configurational complexity but often require substantial computational effort. 41 More tractable multireference methods would have broad implications for modeling catalysis 43, energy conversion 48, and biological systems. 41

The versatility of deep neural networks provides a route to approximate correlated many-electron wavefunctions directly, including those that are strongly correlated. In deep quantum Monte Carlo (deep QMC), a neural network wavefunction is optimized through variational Monte Carlo, allowing electron correlation to be described without relying on an approximate exchange-correlation functional or a truncated coupled-cluster expansion. For example, FermiNet 34 and Psiformer 44 construct determinants from learned orbitals that depend on the full electronic configuration, while PauliNet augments a multireference Hartree-Fock baseline with neural-network Jastrow factors and backflow transformations 16. Obtaining accurate wavefunctions nevertheless requires us to optimize wavefunction parameters separately for each new target, motivating methods that reuse learned electronic structures across related systems.

Transferable neural wavefunctions seek to reduce this repeated computational effort by sharing learned representations across molecular systems. A model pretrained across multiple geometries and compositions can provide initialization for subsequent variational optimization, which potentially reduces the compute required to obtain an accurate wavefunction for a new target. Early work demonstrated parameter sharing across nuclear geometries 40. Subsequent work introduced a transferable mapping from Hartree-Fock orbitals to correlated neural orbitals, demonstrating that pretraining on smaller molecules could accelerate calculations on larger compounds 39. Orbformer subsequently scaled chemical pretraining to 22,350 molecular structures and demonstrated adaptation to bond dissociation and reaction processes 11.

Extending this framework to transition-metal chemistry requires broader chemical coverage and explicit control of total spin. Orbformer’s published pretraining curriculum, named the Light Atom Curriculum (LAC), comprises H, Li, B, C, N, O, F 11. In transition-metal compounds, the relative energies and electronic character of low-lying spin states can change during bond formation and dissociation. Comparing these states requires wavefunctions with the intended total spin. Specifying the numbers of spin-up and spin-down electrons fixes the spin projection (MSM_{S}), but does not generally enforce the total spin (SS). Consequently, energy minimization can favor a lower-energy state with unintended spin character, compromising the calculation of spin-state gaps and the interpretation of reaction pathways. The spin-adapted antisymmetrization method (SAAM) addresses this problem by jointly antisymmetrizing a neural spatial function and a prescribed spin eigenfunction, preserving the target total spin by construction 23.

Extending chemical coverage to heavier atoms also increases the computational burden of treating electrons explicitly. Effective core potentials (ECPs) provide an established route to reducing the computational cost of deep QMC by replacing selected core electrons with effective electron-ion interactions 2, 25. Semilocal effective core potentials have been incorporated into FermiNet 25, while local pseudo-Hamiltonians can further reduce computational cost by avoiding nonlocal integration, enabling calculations on iron–sulfur clusters 12. These developments motivate incorporating ECPs into a chemically pretrained, explicitly spin-adapted architecture.

Here, we introduce SATE, a spin-adapted transferable neural wavefunction architecture with effective core potentials. SATE combines Orbformer’s spatial representation, SAAM-based spin adaptation, and effective-core Hamiltonians in a common neural network architecture. We pretrain the model across an expanded chemical curriculum and investigate whether it provides useful initializations for spin-adapted calculations on compositions excluded from pretraining. We then use molecular-fragment energy differences to test the resulting wavefunctions with chemical observables. By combining broader chemical coverage with explicit control over total spin, SATE provides a framework for comparing molecular energies across geometries, compositions, and spin states.

Results

SATE: an architecture for transferable spin-adapted wavefunctions

Our wavefunction combines Orbformer’s nuclear-conditioned spatial representation 11 with spin-adapted antisymmetrization 23 and correlation-consistent effective core potentials 2. A nuclear message-passing network constructs features from nuclear species and geometry. The features condition both the electron transformer and the orbital generator. The transformer produces a feature vector for each electron that depends on the surrounding nuclei and the positions of all electrons (Figure 1).

Transferability comes from using shared neural-network parameters to generate orbitals conditioned on the nuclear configuration. Multi-system pretraining teaches the network representations that can be used as a starting point for new molecules.

Specifying the number of up- and down-spin electrons fixes the spin projection MSM_{S}, but generally does not fix the total spin SS. Following SAAM 23, we construct the wavefunction by combining spatial functions with prescribed spin eigenfunctions and antisymmetrizing jointly in space and spin (Figure 2):

ΨθS,MS=eJθ​∑k,tctK​𝒜^​[Gθ(k)​ΘtS,MS].\Psi_{\theta}^{S,M_{S}}=e^{J_{\theta}}\sum_{k,t}\frac{c_{t}}{K}\,\hat{\mathcal{A}}\left[G_{\theta}^{(k)}\Theta_{t}^{S,M_{S}}\right].

Each prescribed function is a fixed linear combination of up/down assignments. We implement each assignment as a mask on the neural spatial matrix and evaluate the resulting determinant. Combining these determinants with the prescribed coupling coefficients produces a spin-adapted wavefunction. When multiple spin-coupling functions with the same target SS and MSM_{S} are retained, their relative weights are learned during optimization.

Evaluation of transferability and spin control

We investigate whether pretraining across a range of chemical systems provides a transferable initialization for spin-adapted neural wavefunctions on new molecular compositions. Pretrained and cold-start calculations assess the optimization required to obtain low-energy wavefunctions on molecular compositions excluded from pretraining. Molecular-fragment energy differences attempt to provide chemical validation of the resulting wavefunctions. Independent evaluations of frozen checkpoints assess reliability of reported energies.

Spin adaptation enforces the prescribed total spin

We first assess total-spin control. For O₂ and Fe+, the spin-adapted wavefunctions retain the prescribed values of ⟨S^2⟩\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle, while the corresponding fixed-MSM_{S} Orbformer-based control calculations exhibit spin contamination, particularly for the lower-spin targets (Table 1). These measurements verify the spin construction independently of the accuracy of the calculated energies.

Pretraining improves component energies at matched adaptation budgets

We compare frozen energies after 20,000 accepted VMC adaptation updates using the same architecture for all initializations. Warm starts use the 100,000-update pretrained checkpoint; HF starts include 2,000 orbital-fitting updates before VMC.

Warm initialization yields lower two-seed mean central energies than random initialization for 20 of 21 distinct components and lower estimates than HF initialization for 13 of 20 components (Figure 4). The HF comparison excludes the O2 triplet estimate with substantial drift during frozen evaluations. Several differences are comparable to their combined uncertainties. Target geometries and active-electron counts are provided in Appendix 5.

Improvements in energy differences depend on error cancellation

Improvements in component energies do not consistently result in more accurate observables (Figure 3; Table 4). For CuH, warm initialization lowers the molecular and Cu-atom energies relative to random initialization by 71.61±62.2071.61\pm 62.20 mHa and 31.59±22.1331.59\pm 22.13 mHa, respectively. These unequal gains produce De=108.70±3.85D_{e}=108.70\pm 3.85 mHa, compared with 68.68±83.6568.68\pm 83.65 mHa from random initialization and a reference of 103.11±1.14103.11\pm 1.14 mHa. For CrH, warm initialization brings the dissociation energy from 162.06±10.40162.06\pm 10.40 to 83.58±4.3383.58\pm 4.33 mHa, close to the reference of 81.51±2.6781.51\pm 2.67 mHa. Pretraining does not improve every observable: the Sc ionization energy has an absolute error of 8.29 mHa, compared with 1.63 mHa from HF initialization.

The corresponding Cu/H2 reaction energy is 65.06±3.8665.06\pm 3.86 mHa, compared with the reference of 71.39±1.1471.39\pm 1.14 mHa. This reaction and the CuH binding energy share molecular and atomic components, so their errors are correlated. The warm Fe+ quartet-sextet gap is 12.02±5.1612.02\pm 5.16 mHa against a reference of 9.119.11 mHa, while the Cr ionization energy is 244.24±2.90244.24\pm 2.90 mHa against 248.66248.66 mHa.

Discussion

Our results show that chemical pretraining can provide useful initializations for spin-adapted calculations on compositions excluded from the training curriculum, including transition-metal systems. At matched adaptation budgets, pretraining yields lower central energy estimates for most of the tested states and fragments, with a more consistent advantage over random initialization than over Hartree–Fock initialization. In its current form, SATE provides a common pretrained starting point for fixed-geometry calculations on atoms, ions, and small molecules at prescribed total spin. Using this approach, we computed spin-state gaps, ionization energies, bond dissociation energies, and the energy of a model reaction. SATE extends transferable wavefunction frameworks to include 3d transition-metal systems while enforcing the prescribed total spin.

In the tested O2 and Fe+ states, SATE retains the prescribed total spin, including for lower-spin targets where fixed-MSM_{S} calculations exhibit spin contamination.

A key next step is to quantify how initialization, model capacity and optimization strategy affect the computational cost of reaching a target accuracy. With reliable accuracy and transfer, a shared pretrained representation can reduce the repeated optimization needed to investigate bond activation, reaction energetics, and competing electronic states. Such calculations could support systematic comparisons of how substitution, charge, and metal ligation alter bonding and reactivity in organic molecules, catalysts, and enzyme active-site models. Studies of organic diradicals 7, iron-oxo catalysis 36, and cytochrome P450 47 illustrate how these chemical changes affect spin-state energetics and bond activation. Beyond molecular applications, SATE could be adapted to periodic boundary conditions, building on prior work on transferable neural wavefunctions for solids 13. Furthermore, combining parameter reuse with total-spin control could support comparisons of competing spin states at semiconductor defects 14.

SATE is designed as a foundation model for spin-resolved electronic structure across chemical space. By combining broader chemical coverage with explicit control over total spin, SATE provides a framework for comparing molecular energies across geometries, compositions, and spin states.

Methods

Transferable spatial representation

The orbital generator supplies feature-to-orbital projection weights and electron-nucleus envelope coefficients. Envelope decay exponents are trainable element-specific parameters shared across orbitals, spatial components, and geometries. For spatial component k, the matrix is:

Mθ(k)=[Hθ​(Wθ(k))𝖳]⊙Ωθ(k).M_{\theta}^{(k)}=\left[H_{\theta}\left(W_{\theta}^{(k)}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\right]\odot\Omega_{\theta}^{(k)}.

where HθH_{\theta} contains the electron features, Wθ(k)W_{\theta}^{(k)} maps the features to orbital values, and Ωθ(k)\Omega_{\theta}^{(k)} are the envelopes. The ⊙\odot symbol is element-wise multiplication. Rows correspond to electrons and columns to spatial orbitals. Since the electron features depend on the complete electron configuration, these are generalized orbitals rather than independent-particle orbitals.

For each doubly occupied spatial orbital, two columns share projection and envelope parameters. The subsequent spin construction associates these copies with opposite spins, allowing double occupation of that orbital. Although the columns are identical in the spatial matrix, their spin factors distinguish them during antisymmetrization. Active orbital columns retain independent parameters rather than being constrained to identical pairs.

Spin-adapted wavefunction

Each spin primitive is a product of one-electron spin functions and is represented computationally by a spin-mask matrix. Fixed linear combinations of these primitives form independent spin-adapted coupling functions with prescribed SS and MSM_{S}. Learned coefficients mix the retained coupling functions, while KK controls the number of spatial components.

Nprimitive=(nana/2−S),Ncoupling=(nana/2−S)−(nana/2−S−1).N_{\mathrm{primitive}}=\binom{n_{\mathrm{a}}}{n_{\mathrm{a}}/2-S},\qquad N_{\mathrm{coupling}}=\binom{n_{\mathrm{a}}}{n_{\mathrm{a}}/2-S}-\binom{n_{\mathrm{a}}}{n_{\mathrm{a}}/2-S-1}.

Here, nan_{a} is the number of active electrons, assuming MS=SM_{S}=S. These functions are used to generate the spin-tables for adaptation and SATE pretraining, counting the complete basis for the chosen active space 23. The pretraining curriculum (Table 3) and transfer benchmarks use spin-coupling bases containing zero to seven active electrons, with the remaining electrons assigned to paired orbitals. Active-electron spins are coupled to the prescribed total spin.

The complete determinant sum has the prescribed total spin, while an individual determinant need not. We evaluate the sum using logarithmic arithmetic and verify spin character by evaluating ⟨S^2⟩\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle. A symmetric, spin-independent Jastrow factor adds correlation without changing total spin.

A complementary approach, spin-adapted neural-network backflow (SA-NNBF), enforces total spin in a second-quantized representation 26.

Hamiltonians and variational optimization

We work within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, fixing the nuclei as point charges. Core electrons are approximated with an effective core potential and the remaining electrons are treated explicitly. In atomic units, the following equation describes the Hamiltonian of an atomic or molecular system:

H^=−12∑i∇i2+∑i<j1ri​j+∑i​AV^AECP+Eion.\hat{H}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\nabla_{i}^{2}+\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{r_{ij}}+\sum_{iA}\hat{V}_{A}^{\mathrm{ECP}}+E_{\mathrm{ion}}.

where ri​jr_{ij} is the electron-electron separation, V^AECP\hat{V}_{A}^{\mathrm{ECP}} contains the local and nonlocal electron-ion interactions at center AA, and EionE_{\mathrm{ion}} is the repulsion between nuclei with their effective charges. The nonlocal terms distinguish angular-momentum channels around each nucleus. For the 3d transition metals, the Ne-core correlation-consistent effective core potentials (ccECPs) replace ten core electrons while retaining the 3​s3s and 3​p3p semicore electrons explicitly, together with the 3​d3d and 4​s4s valence electrons 2. Spin-orbit coupling is omitted, so the Hamiltonian commutes with the total-spin operator S^2\hat{S}^{2}. Molecular and fragment energies are calculated using the same effective-core Hamiltonian. During pretraining, hydrogen was treated all-electron. For the other curriculum systems, ccECPs were used 2, 4, 5, 45. In the evaluation panel, O2, C, N, O, and H2 were treated all-electron, while transition-metal centers used ten-electron-core ccECPs.

For a wavefunction Ψθ\Psi_{\theta} with parameters θ\theta, variational Monte Carlo estimates the energy expectation

Eθ=⟨Ψθ|H^|Ψθ⟩⟨Ψθ|Ψθ⟩=Eπθ​[EL]E_{\theta}=\frac{\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\hat{H}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}=E_{\pi_{\theta}}[E_{L}]

where,

πθ​(r)=|Ψθ​(r)|2Zθ,EL​(r)=(H^​Ψθ)​(r)Ψθ​(r).\pi_{\theta}(r)=\frac{|\Psi_{\theta}(r)|^{2}}{Z_{\theta}},\qquad E_{L}(r)=\frac{(\hat{H}\Psi_{\theta})(r)}{\Psi_{\theta}(r)}.

Here rr denotes the complete set of electron coordinates and ZθZ_{\theta} is the normalization integral.

Markov-chain electron position sampling of configurations estimates the energy and its parameter gradients. During optimization, changes to θ\theta also change the target distribution πθ\pi_{\theta}. We optimize the wavefunction parameters using Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (KFAC) 28. Spatial derivatives required for the kinetic energy are evaluated using forward Laplacian automatic differentiation 24 (see Appendix 1).

Pretraining and adaptation protocol

Pretraining used 1 molecule per NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell graphics processing unit (GPU). 32 of the same GPUs were used with 256 walkers per molecule for a total of 8,192 walkers. Adaptation uses 1,024 walkers on one GPU for its target system. Table 2 compares the architecture and protocol with SAAM and Orbformer.

The pretrained model was initialized randomly and without HF fitting. Warm adaptations initialized neural parameters from the specified pretrained checkpoint, with fresh optimizer and walker states. Random controls used freshly initialized neural parameters. HF controls underwent 2,000 orbital-fitting updates before VMC, using aug-cc-pVDZ for all-electron targets and ccECP-cc-pVTZ for ccECP targets.

Electron configurations were sampled using random-walk Metropolis. Random-walk Metropolis uses displacement proposals with an acceptance-rejection step 29, 15.

All energy-comparing runs use 16 determinant spatial components and a linear learning-rate warmup of 10−7→10−310^{-7}\to 10^{-3} over 500 updates. After the 500-update warmup, the learning rate follows an inverse-time scale of 10,000 updates. We use KFAC damping of 10−310^{-3}, KFAC norm constraint of 10−310^{-3}, curvature moving-average decay of 0.95, median-centered local-energy clipping of 5×5\times mean absolute deviation from median for optimization, 12 point ccECP angular quadrature, and 32-bit floating-point (FP32) parameters and local energies.

Independent energy evaluation

For the transfer-energy comparisons in Figures 3 and 4, all learned parameters are held fixed after 20,000 adaptation updates. Each adaptation seed is evaluated using two separately seeded persistent Metropolis chains initialized from saved walkers. Each uses 256 walkers, 1,200 burn-in sweeps, and 512 measurement records separated by 60 sweeps. Reported energies combine the FP32 mean with a paired FP64 correction evaluated on identical configurations every sixteenth record (Appendix 2).

All sampled local energies are retained. Time-blocking accounts for serially correlated measurements 10. For each checkpoint, we use the largest uncertainty estimate from the time-blocking and between-chain variation, adding the uncertainty in the FP64-FP32 correction. Component uncertainties are propagated to energy differences. These estimates exclude optimization and Hamiltonian approximation errors.

Observables and reference conventions

We evaluate bond dissociation energies, spin-state gaps, ionization energies, and reaction energy from their component energies. Electronic dissociation energies, DeD_{e}, are calculated as the sum of the separated-atom energies minus the molecular energy. Spin-state gaps are the energy of the first state named minus the second; for O2 and Fe+, these are singlet minus triplet and quartet minus sextet, respectively. Ionization energies are calculated as cation minus neutral-atom energies.

Atomic spectroscopic reference data are available from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database 22 and the NIST Handbook 38. The tabulated Fe+, Cr, C, N, and O spin-gap references are reproduced, to the shown precision, by differences of term centroids E¯=∑J(2​J+1)​EJ/∑J(2​J+1)\bar{E}=\sum_{J}(2J+1)E_{J}/\sum_{J}(2J+1) using the Handbook levels. The CuH dissociation reference is the conversion of De=22 630±250​cm−1D_{e}=22\,630\pm 250\,\mathrm{cm}^{-1} reported by Mohammadian and Shayesteh 31. Electronic well depths DeD_{e}, zero-point dissociation energies D0D_{0}, and finite-temperature bond dissociation enthalpies must be distinguished when using experimental thermochemistry and spectroscopic constants 27, 37, 19.

Appendix 1: Forward Laplacian

Forward Laplacian calculates the derivatives of a neural network’s intermediate features Δ​𝐡l\Delta\mathbf{h}^{l} and output y=log⁡|Ψθ|y=\log|\Psi_{\theta}| with respect to the electron positions xx avoiding constructing the full Hessian. Instead, Δ​y\Delta y is computed directly using the first derivatives and the intermediate Laplacian term 24.

[𝐱∇𝐱Δ​𝐱]→⋯→[𝐡l∇𝐡lΔ​𝐡l]→⋯→[y∇yΔ​y]\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}\\ \nabla\mathbf{x}\\ \Delta\mathbf{x}\end{bmatrix}\to\cdots\to\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{h}^{l}\\ \nabla\mathbf{h}^{l}\\ \Delta\mathbf{h}^{l}\end{bmatrix}\to\cdots\to\begin{bmatrix}y\\ \nabla y\\ \Delta y\end{bmatrix}

The table compares loop-based and forward-Laplacian evaluation times.

System Loop time (s) Forward time (s) Time reduction
CuH 3.707 2.76 25.55%
ScCl 4.898 3.995 18.44%

We compare loop-based and forward-Laplacian local-energy evaluation on identical fixed electron configurations using FP64 arithmetic. Timings correspond to a 32-configuration batch, rather than a complete optimization update.

Appendix 2: FP64 Correction

We evaluate frozen checkpoints primarily in FP32 to reduce computational cost and optimize calculations for NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwells. Every 16th measurement record is also evaluated in FP64 using the same electron configurations and unchanged model parameters. The mean difference between these paired evaluations corrects the FP32 energy:

Ereported=E¯FP32+EFP64−EFP32¯paired.E_{\mathrm{reported}}=\overline{E}_{\mathrm{FP32}}+\overline{E_{\mathrm{FP64}}-E_{\mathrm{FP32}}}_{\mathrm{paired}}.

Statistical uncertainties account for correlations between successive measurements and differences between the two sampling streams. The uncertainty in the precision correction is added to the FP32 uncertainty.

Appendix 3: Finetuning vs Cold Training Results

HF starts include 2,000 orbital-fitting updates before VMC. All columns use the same architecture. Cold columns average adaptation seeds 42 and 43; uncertainties use the larger of the propagated Monte Carlo and between-seed standard errors. Observables are calculated within each seed before averaging. Pretrained-column uncertainties are Monte Carlo standard errors for individual runs. Independent component uncertainties are propagated in quadrature; E⁡(H)=−0.5E(\mathrm{H})=-0.5 Ha. All frozen measurements use persistent Metropolis chains. †\dagger The HF O2 triplet includes a read with substantial energy drift during frozen measurement.

Appendix 4: Curriculum Provenance

The 5,073 source-derived configurations include 46 identity-corrected LAC configurations and two reconstructed primary spectroscopic parents. A further 19,927 configurations are generated distortions. The symbols rer_{e}, r0r_{0}, rar_{a}, and rgr_{g} distinguish equilibrium, effective ground-state, and diffraction-derived distance conventions. Additional spin sectors are prescribed vertical-spin training targets at unchanged nuclear coordinates. For 46 configurations derived from the LAC vinyl-fluoride parent, we corrected an atomic-number assignment from nitrogen to fluorine, consistent with the parent’s reference geometry.

Appendix 5: Evaluation Targets

nan_{\mathrm{a}} specifies the number of active electrons in the spin-coupling construction. The remaining explicitly treated electrons are assigned to paired spatial orbitals.

For the 20,000-update energy comparisons, both O2 spin states use the same distance of 1.2 Å, whereas the spectroscopic reference is adiabatic 20.

The calculations in Table 1 were randomly initialized and optimized for 10,000 updates. Both methods used O2 bond lengths of 1.2156 Å for the singlet and 1.20752 Å for the triplet. SATE used two active electrons for both O2 states and seven for both Fe+ states.
